LEARNING PATH LESSON · WEATHER, SEASONS & WHAT WE WEAR · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Weather Forecast — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the morning forecast into a family ritual: what forecasts are, who makes them, how to read the little icons, and how the sky’s plan decides the coat, the hat and the day.

What is this?

A weather forecast is a careful prediction of what the sky will do next — today, tomorrow, all week. Weather scientists read maps, clouds and instruments, then share the plan on TV, radio and phones.

What does it mean?

Forecasts turn unknown skies into known plans: rain icon means the wellies come out, sun icon means the sun hat, storm warning means the family stays close to home. The forecast does not control the sky — it just reads the clues early.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three forecast ideas: the forecast tells us what the sky plans before it happens; sun, cloud and rain icons are the forecast’s picture words; and families use the forecast to choose clothes and to stay safe when big weather comes.

Why this matters

Checking the forecast is daily evidence-based decision-making in child-size form: information → choice → action → check the result. Children adore grading the forecaster’s homework — and grading an adult’s work respectfully is a genuine critical-thinking exercise.

What it teaches

Prediction and verification, icon literacy, planning and sequencing (what comes first — coat or boots?), weather vocabulary across days (today, tomorrow, the whole week), and the family-habit feeling that preparation beats surprise.

Words to learn

forecastpredictweather reporterplanicontomorrowweeklystorm warning

Say this to your child

“"The weather reporter looks at the sky’s clues and tells us the plan: rain or sun, warm or cold, windy or calm. We listen to the forecast, then we get ready — the right clothes, the right bag, the right day."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "A weather forecast is the sky’s plan, told to us before it happens."
  2. Read the picture: the presenter in a yellow blazer points at a big weather map, a board with two thermometers reading 18 degrees, a rain-cloud board, a rail with a yellow raincoat, a blue jacket and a purple jumper, a "Tomorrow" board with a sun behind a cloud, and a five-day chart from Monday to Friday with sun and cloud icons.
  3. Play icon-reading: show today’s forecast on your phone — sun, cloud or rain? Ask your child to "read" it back to you like a story.
  4. Let the forecast dress you both: rain icon → raincoat and boots; sun icon → sun hat. Make the choice out loud so the reasoning is heard.
  5. crown the family weather reporter: once a week, your child presents the weather — paper-tube microphone, big gestures, the works.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a TV weather presenter in a yellow blazer stands in a studio: she presents a huge weather map with clouds and coloured weather lines, points at a board with two thermometers reading 18°C, shows a board with a big rain cloud and raindrops, stands beside a clothes rail holding a yellow rain jacket, a blue jacket and a purple jumper, points to a "Tomorrow" card showing a sun behind a cloud, and presents a weekly chart — Monday sunny, Tuesday rain, Wednesday cloud, Thursday partly sunny, Friday sunny — with a temperature number under each day.

Ask your child

"What does the weather reporter tell us?" "What do we take outside if the forecast says rain?" "What does the sun icon mean?" "Did yesterday’s forecast get it right?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The forecast says rain — boots please!" or deliver a full bulletin: "Today is cloudy, tomorrow is sunny — that is the weather, thank you!"

Out in the real world

Make the morning forecast check a fixed ritual — while shoes go on, the sky’s plan gets read. Let your child spot forecast icons on phones, roadside signs, newspapers and TV. After big-weather days, hold the verdict together: right sky, wrong sky, half right?

Try it together

Weather studio: a cardboard TV frame, a paper-tube microphone and yesterday’s drawings as props — your child presents today, tomorrow and "the weekend", complete with sound effects. Then the forecast-vs-reality chart: two columns, sticker for every correct call.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who tells us the sky’s plan? What do we grab when the forecast says rain? What do we do when a big storm is forecast?" Reporter, raincoat, stay home together — planning is now a family skill.

Parent tips

Never pretend forecasts are perfect — the misses are teachable gold: "The sky changed its mind; even weather scientists keep learning." And keep the ritual tiny: one icon, one clothing choice, ten seconds. Rituals that survive are rituals that stay small.

Staying safe

Teach the storm-warning response explicitly: when grown-ups say a big storm is coming, we stay indoors, away from windows, and let the wild sky pass. Children can help — fetching the torch, counting the batteries — because helping prepares, and preparing calms.

This lesson pairs with the Weather Forecast flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Weather, Seasons & What We Wear (Class 34).
